title: The absurd theatre of Russia's choice-free election
gist: Egor Sokolov describes Russia's 18-20 September 2026 Duma election as a choice-free 'spin dictatorship' exercise: United Russia won ~58% after Yabloko, the only anti-war party (polled by independent sociologists at ~20%), was struck off on absurd grounds, monitoring was crushed, and unmonitorable online voting was used in 33 of 89 regions. He argues the regime is drifting from spin toward a 'fear dictatorship' and that latent anti-war sentiment is significant.

themes.theme: Election results and suppressed anti-war sentiment

insights.claim: United Russia won a majority for the fifth time with nearly 58% of the vote; the Communists got just under 14%, the far-right LDPR 9%, New People 8% and Just Russia 5%.
insights.speaker: Egor Sokolov
insights.so_what: Confirms regime continuity and no domestic political constraint on the war in the near term.
insights.quote: receiving nearly 58 per cent of the votes

insights.claim: Independent sociologists estimated that Yabloko, as the only party cautiously calling for an end to the war, could have come second with about 20% of the vote before it was removed by a court two weeks after registration.
insights.speaker: Egor Sokolov
insights.so_what: Suggests meaningful latent anti-war sentiment in Russia, a hidden variable for war duration and post-Putin scenarios.
insights.quote: according to independent sociologists, it could have come second with around 20 per cent of the vote

insights.claim: The regime removed Yabloko mainly because its participation would have legitimised calls for peace, which can lead to prison in contemporary Russia.
insights.speaker: Egor Sokolov
insights.so_what: The Kremlin sees peace advocacy as an existential threat, implying low appetite for negotiated settlement driven from within.
insights.quote: would have legitimised calls for peace – for which one can actually be sent to prison in contemporary Russia

insights.claim: The legal grounds for removing Yabloko were copyright claims over the phrases 'Let There Always Be Sunshine' and 'If Only There Were No War' and about £140 of 'foreign funding' from Russians abroad.
insights.speaker: Egor Sokolov
insights.so_what: Illustrates the arbitrariness of Russian legal processes, relevant to rule-of-law risk.

themes.theme: Regime type: from spin to fear dictatorship

insights.claim: Putinism built an implicitly choice-free system mimicking democratic institutions, which Guriev and Treisman term a 'spin dictatorship'.
insights.speaker: Egor Sokolov
insights.so_what: Useful lens for reading Russian political signals as managed outputs rather than genuine preferences.
insights.locator: While that was an explicitly choice-free system

insights.claim: Since the invasion of Ukraine, Putinism has been rapidly moving toward a 20th-century 'fear dictatorship' relying more on violence than manipulation, though the electoral machine still runs on spin logic for now.
insights.speaker: Egor Sokolov
insights.so_what: Increasing repression raises long-term regime-instability and sanctions-persistence risk.
insights.quote: since the invasion of Ukraine, Putinism has been rapidly moving back to the future, towards the 20th-century ‘fear dictatorships’
insights.locator: While that was an explicitly choice-free system

insights.claim: United Russia's victory demonstrates the bureaucracy's ability to deliver the required result while maintaining minimal electoral formalities, not Putin's popularity.
insights.speaker: Egor Sokolov
insights.so_what: Do not read Russian electoral results as evidence of genuine popular support for the war.

insights.claim: If democratic politics ever re-emerge in Russia, the author expects any heirs to Putinism to be thoroughly discredited by both the regime's crimes and its absurdity.
insights.speaker: Egor Sokolov
insights.so_what: Implies a potential sharp political break in any post-Putin transition.

insights.claim: Political competition has been systematically destroyed over 25 years; Navalny failed to register his party in nine attempts between 2013 and 2019.
insights.speaker: Egor Sokolov
insights.so_what: Absence of any organised opposition reduces the probability of orderly political change.

themes.theme: Digital election manipulation and monitoring collapse

insights.claim: Online voting was used in 33 of Russia's 89 regions in 2026 and is a black box that cannot be monitored at all.
insights.speaker: Egor Sokolov
insights.so_what: E-voting gives the state an untraceable lever over outcomes, a model other autocracies may copy.
insights.quote: The system is a black box that only produces a result
insights.locator: Finally, as a sign of the times

insights.claim: In Moscow's 2021 elections, opposition candidates led on paper ballots in eight of 15 districts, but online voting reversed the result in every case in favour of United Russia.
insights.speaker: Egor Sokolov
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that digital voting can overturn paper outcomes.
insights.quote: online voting changed the result in every case and secured a victory for United Russia
insights.locator: Finally, as a sign of the times

insights.claim: Extending elections to three days since 2020 means no observer can watch ballot boxes throughout, while monitor Golos was labelled a foreign agent and co-chair Grigory Melkonyants imprisoned.
insights.speaker: Egor Sokolov
insights.so_what: Institutional design changes are dismantling any external check on results.

insights.claim: Days before the vote, Russian AI assistant Alice predicted United Russia would win 324 seats, which turned out to be 31 seats short of the actual result.
insights.speaker: Egor Sokolov
insights.so_what: Signals the outcome was predetermined and that state-aligned AI products echo official narratives.
insights.quote: it underestimated United Russia’s result by an impressive 31 seats
